exhibits.title: ECB: Repeated Blocks
exhibits.action: Encrypt repeating text or an uploaded image with ECB.
exhibits.outcome: Compare ciphertext blocks and an image view that preserves repeated-block structure; decrypting one tampered ciphertext block illustrates absent authentication.
exhibits.limits: Educational mode implementation; ECB has no integrity check and is inappropriate for multi-block secret data.

exhibits.title: CBC: Chaining, IVs and Bit Flips
exhibits.action: Encrypt with CBC, test IV reuse or the targeted bit-flip puzzle, then decrypt with correct and modified inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect chained blocks and how IV reuse reveals shared prefixes or ciphertext modification changes decrypted bytes without an integrity guarantee.
exhibits.limits: CBC alone provides confidentiality, not authenticity; the padding-oracle attack is covered in a separate lab.

exhibits.title: GCM Nonce-Reuse Forgery
exhibits.action: Edit two one-block plaintexts and a forged target, then run reused-nonce recovery and the fresh-nonce control.
exhibits.outcome: Display recovered GHASH subkey H, recovered tag mask, forged ciphertext and tag, and whether WebCrypto AES-GCM accepts the forged message.
exhibits.limits: The worked algebra uses two equal-length single-block ciphertexts with empty AAD; it does not recover the AES encryption key, and the fresh-nonce control should reject.

exhibits.title: GCM Authenticated Encryption
exhibits.action: Enter plaintext and AAD, select a tag length, encrypt and try wrong AAD, wrong nonce or a flipped ciphertext bit.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect ciphertext and tag; WebCrypto rejects decryption after unauthenticated changes.
exhibits.limits: Correct use requires unique nonces per key; a shorter tag reduces forgery resistance and may require specific message-length and usage limits.

exhibits.title: Padding Oracle Attack
exhibits.action: Enter a secret plaintext, set up a CBC padding oracle, and run byte-wise attack queries.
exhibits.outcome: Watch padding-validity queries and recovered plaintext bytes with a query counter.
exhibits.limits: The laboratory intentionally exposes a padding-validity signal; it is not inherent to every CBC deployment.

exhibits.title: Same plaintext, all seven modes
exhibits.action: Enter repeated-block plaintext and click “Encrypt under all 7 modes.”
exhibits.outcome: Compare seven ciphertext block grids for ECB, CBC, CTR, OFB, CFB, GCM and CCM; repeated ECB blocks are marked.
exhibits.limits: A side-by-side block grid illustrates one property; it is not a comprehensive security proof. CBC, CTR, OFB and CFB remain confidentiality-only; GCM and CCM include authentication.

exhibits.title: Run BB84 with or without intercept-resend Eve
exhibits.action: Choose photon count, noise and QBER threshold, then run without Eve and with a full intercept-resend Eve; inspect the animated photon sample and sifting table.
exhibits.outcome: The classical model displays sent, sifted and sacrificed counts and observed QBER; an ideal noiseless full-interception run tends toward 25% QBER, while sample results vary.
exhibits.limits: No photons or quantum states are produced. This models one Eve strategy and does not calculate a finite-key secrecy proof or guarantee detecting every eavesdropper.

exhibits.title: Estimate errors and decide whether to abort
exhibits.action: Adjust channel noise or the QBER threshold and repeat; inspect the sacrificed-bit error count and decision gauge.
exhibits.outcome: The run aborts at or above the chosen threshold and discards the key, including when noise alone causes excess disturbance; below it the demonstration continues.
exhibits.limits: The threshold is a teaching control, not a derived security bound. Alice and Bob see disturbance, not its cause.

exhibits.title: Hash retained bits and try AES-GCM
exhibits.action: After an accepted simulated exchange, inspect Alice's and Bob's separately SHA-256-derived keys and encrypt a message using Alice's key.
exhibits.outcome: AES-GCM decryption with Bob's key succeeds when the retained bits agree and rejects when residual bit disagreements produce a different key.
exhibits.limits: The cryptographic hash and AEAD run for real on bits generated by a classical BB84 simulation; the main run omits reconciliation and privacy amplification. Hashing does not create secrecy or prove Eve's knowledge is small.

exhibits.title: Try public reconciliation and conditional extraction
exhibits.action: Supply a hypothetical conditional min-entropy lower bound after an accepted run and press Try post-processing.
exhibits.outcome: The teaching model publishes Hamming syndromes and a 16-bit verification tag, attempts one correction per seven-bit block, subtracts public leakage and a margin from the assumed entropy budget, then may apply a public-seeded Toeplitz extractor or output zero bits.
exhibits.limits: The supplied entropy bound is not inferred from QBER. The model is not a finite-key QKD proof, and its extracted bits are not used for the main AES-256 key.

exhibits.title: Compare receipt-first and early-basis schedules
exhibits.action: Choose Bob confirms receipt first or Alice reveals bases too early and compare the exact four-state enumeration under the specified Eve.
exhibits.outcome: With Eve permitted to store each qubit until an early basis announcement, the modeled Eve learns the sifted bits without induced QBER; receipt-first forces a basis choice before the announcement and reveals the usual full-intercept disturbance.
exhibits.limits: This exact enumeration is for a deliberately specified attack and timing assumption, not a general proof that receipt-first alone secures QKD.

exhibits.title: Commit, open, and try to cheat
exhibits.action: Commit a message with a fresh salt, then open the published SHA-256 commitment honestly or with a changed message.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier accepts a matching opening and rejects the changed opening, with the commitment and comparison shown.
exhibits.limits: One failed tampering attempt illustrates binding; it is not a proof that collisions cannot be found.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 — Commit, Open, and Try to Cheat

exhibits.title: Binding, quantified
exhibits.action: Run a batch of 3,000 alternative-opening trials against a fixed SHA-256 commitment.
exhibits.outcome: The collision-search result and an order-of-magnitude meter compare attempts with a generic 2^128 collision-work benchmark.
exhibits.limits: The button actually searches alternatives against one fixed commitment, a harder fixed-target trial; the generic 2^128 benchmark is for unrestricted birthday collisions. The finite trial cannot establish binding.

exhibits.title: Hiding and how it breaks
exhibits.action: Sample salted commitments to 0 and 1, toggle a computationally unbounded attacker, then build an unblinded SHA-256(message) and run a small dictionary attack.
exhibits.outcome: One sampled digest-bit frequency chart, conditional hash-versus-Pedersen hiding explanation, and a candidate recovery verdict show what salt contributes.
exhibits.limits: A single sampled output bit cannot prove indistinguishability; the unbounded-attacker toggle is explanatory, while Pedersen's guarantee assumes a uniform secret scalar.

exhibits.title: Pedersen commitments and additive homomorphism
exhibits.action: Commit and open one numeric message, then add commitments to two messages without opening either first.
exhibits.outcome: Live P-256 point checks validate openings and the homomorphic sum; an SVG shows a schematic tip-to-tail analogy.
exhibits.limits: Actual point arithmetic uses P-256; SVG placement is schematic. The teaching hash-to-point derivation is not an RFC 9380 production suite and code is unaudited.

exhibits.title: Sealed-bid auction
exhibits.action: Set three bids, publish their salted commitments, then reveal and verify all openings.
exhibits.outcome: The sealed table opens and displays the verified winning bid.
exhibits.limits: All participants are assumed to reveal; production auctions require deadlines and non-reveal rules.

exhibits.title: Coin flip and selective abort
exhibits.action: Commit Bob's bit, choose Alice's bit, then open honestly, attempt a changed bit, or selectively withhold an unfavorable opening.
exhibits.outcome: XOR results, rejected changes, aborted rounds, and a four-case table show that binding does not prevent selective abort bias.
exhibits.limits: This is a toy two-party workflow; a real protocol needs abort handling.
exhibits.section: Coin flip: a committed bit can still be withheld

exhibits.title: Curve Explorer
exhibits.action: Switch between smooth real-number geometry and a finite field of 17; select points P and Q on the plotted curve.
exhibits.outcome: See the third intersection, reflection and resulting P+Q, with finite-field line segments wrapping modulo 17.
exhibits.limits: Tiny teaching field and real-number picture are analogies; production curves have large finite fields.

exhibits.title: Break the Discrete Log
exhibits.action: Generate a new toy secret and solve its public point by brute force.
exhibits.outcome: Watch candidate scalar multiples until the small-curve private scalar is found.
exhibits.limits: Toy small-field brute force does not estimate practical attacks on production curves.

exhibits.title: ECDH Live Demo
exhibits.action: Choose a supported real curve, generate fresh Alice and Bob keypairs, and inspect their public values and shared outputs.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the matching raw shared value Z and the transcript from both parties; an X25519-only expandable note explains low-order all-zero rejection.
exhibits.limits: Private scalars are intentionally displayed for teaching; Z is not yet an application key and must go through a KDF. The panel generates valid peer keys and does not test attacker-supplied low-order inputs.

exhibits.title: Scalar Multiplication
exhibits.action: Switch between a small field and supported real curve, change scalar, and inspect the resulting public point.
exhibits.outcome: See an exact small-field double-and-add trace and a real curve result with its actual output encoding.
exhibits.limits: The trace is for the toy field only; X25519 uses a Montgomery ladder and real short-Weierstrass implementations use different optimized algorithms. JavaScript timing is not a side-channel guarantee.

exhibits.title: Curve Comparison
exhibits.action: Read parameter and subgroup information across the supported curves.
exhibits.outcome: Compare named curve families and their metadata alongside small-field analogy plots.
exhibits.limits: Mini-plots are small-field analogies, not production-field points; no quantum attack is executed.

exhibits.title: Seal a Document
exhibits.action: Choose an ML-DSA parameter set, generate keys, enter document text, seal and verify the exported JSON; tamper with the text and verify again.
exhibits.outcome: The browser signs the document content with FIPS 204 ML-DSA and verifies it under the included public key. Recomputing an ordinary SHA-256 content hash after an edit cannot make the old ML-DSA signature verify.
exhibits.limits: The JSON package signs only content. The signer label and timestamp are unsigned, and its included public key is not bound to a trusted human identity; successful verification alone does not establish signer identity.

exhibits.title: Choosing a parameter set
exhibits.action: Read the protocol and policy questions and compare ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 by NIST strength category, key size and signature size.
exhibits.outcome: The panel explains how interoperability requirements and security category guide a parameter choice; it does not run ML-DSA internals in this section.
exhibits.limits: This is conceptual guidance and a static FIPS parameter table. It does not establish a one-size-fits-all best parameter set or run signing inside the guidance panel.

exhibits.title: Signature Size Comparison
exhibits.action: Compare the signature-size bars for RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.
exhibits.outcome: The page draws bars from specified byte counts; its ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 counts are FIPS 204 Table 2 values, not fresh signatures computed by this chart.
exhibits.limits: This chart visualizes transcribed specification sizes. Separate signing and benchmark controls perform real ML-DSA operations.

exhibits.title: Run an E91 Bell test
exhibits.action: Choose an ideal, intercept-resend Eve, noisy, misaligned, or lossy channel; choose pair count and seed; run the simulation.
exhibits.outcome: The page samples singlet-pair measurements and displays measured CHSH |S|, a conservative joint 95% interval, expected correlations and candidate sifted-key agreement.
exhibits.limits: A Bell violation under this idealized model is not a QKD key-security proof; the lab omits authenticated discussion, reconciliation, privacy amplification, finite-key security, and realistic device behavior.

exhibits.title: Vary Eve, depolarization, alignment, and loss
exhibits.action: Switch between channel scenarios and adjust their parameter slider, then compare measured Bell correlations, coincidence rates, and candidate-key agreement.
exhibits.outcome: Intercept-resend uses a fixed Eve basis, depolarization randomly replaces a pair, fixed analyzer offset shifts Bob's angle, and independent photon loss reduces coincident rounds.
exhibits.limits: These are specified textbook channel models, not evidence that every eavesdropper is detected. Loss is independent and fair-sampling behavior is assumed.

exhibits.title: What an elliptic curve is
exhibits.action: Read the Weierstrass equation and inspect the rendered real-curve construction.
exhibits.outcome: The smooth curve, mirrored points, point at infinity, and finite-field bridge are shown.
exhibits.limits: Introductory geometric explanation; the displayed real curve is not a cryptographic group.

exhibits.title: Point addition over the reals
exhibits.action: Drag P and Q, toggle doubling or reflection, or choose the inverse and y=0 example chips.
exhibits.outcome: The chord or tangent and algebraic sum update, including P + (-P) = O and 2P = O edge cases.
exhibits.limits: Floating-point geometry over the reals illustrates the group law; cryptographic arithmetic is over finite fields.

exhibits.title: Point addition over a finite field
exhibits.action: Switch to the finite-field tab and select P and Q on a small lattice or choose secp256k1 preset points.
exhibits.outcome: Exact modular point sums and special cases appear; secp256k1 gives a numeric readout instead of an impossible lattice plot.
exhibits.limits: Small lattices are teaching curves; secp256k1 coordinates are computed numerically, not plotted.

exhibits.title: Scalar multiplication: k · P
exhibits.action: Choose a curve, k, and repeated-addition or double-and-add method; step or play the trace.
exhibits.outcome: The point accumulator, binary-bit trace, and operation counts expose the O(k) versus O(log k) gap and order edge cases.
exhibits.limits: Naive addition is capped at k=2000 to keep the browser responsive.

exhibits.title: Why you cannot go backwards (ECDLP)
exhibits.action: Choose a new hidden scalar and step or play successive multiples of G on the F97 teaching curve.
exhibits.outcome: The walk locates Q=kG after k steps and compares the toy group with the approximate generic attack cost for secp256k1.
exhibits.limits: The interactive walk is a 99-element toy subgroup, not an actual solver for a cryptographic curve; generic square-root cost is explanatory.

exhibits.title: Envelope Operations
exhibits.action: Create a KEK, enter plaintext and context, seal and open an envelope, change tenant context, rotate the KEK and re-wrap.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the envelope and operation timeline; changing the authenticated context makes AES-GCM opening fail, while key version rotation and re-wrap are visible.
exhibits.limits: The payload context is GCM AAD; RFC 3394 wrapping does not accept separate AAD. In-browser key storage is not a hosted KMS or HSM.

exhibits.title: Who may use this key?
exhibits.action: Run the same wrapped DEK through a log-only decrypt API and an opt-in caller/key/operation grant.
exhibits.outcome: Compare unauthorized Mallory receiving a DEK from an unguarded API, denial by a grant check, and allowed Alice unwrapping the same DEK.
exhibits.limits: Alice and Mallory are caller-supplied labels; no login, verified IAM principal, HSM, or real non-extractable key boundary.

exhibits.title: Steal one KEK: what still opens?
exhibits.action: Choose isolated tenant KEKs or one shared KEK, then run the compromise experiment.
exhibits.outcome: Read actual successful decrypt counts for archived copies, current wraps, retained DEKs, future data and owner access across maintenance stages.
exhibits.limits: Attacker holds stolen raw KEK material and archived envelopes, with no further KMS API access; results do not imply re-wrapping erases archived plaintext.
exhibits.section: Steal one KEK: what still opens?

exhibits.title: Illustrative signing and public-key-only forgery
exhibits.action: Generate an illustrative keypair, sign and verify a message, run the tamper test, then try the short-vector forgery with only the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a generated signature and norm check; message tampering is rejected, while the short-vector forgery may pass this panel's illustrative verifier because the signer never uses the private trapdoor.
exhibits.limits: This panel's signing flow is intentionally forgeable and is not Falcon or an unforgeability demonstration; it never reads the private trapdoor. The real Falcon WASM run is a separate panel.

exhibits.title: Simulated sampler timing and correlation attack
exhibits.section: Panel 5 — Side-Channels, Use Cases, and Warnings
exhibits.action: Toggle leaky versus constant-time simulated sampler, run 512 samples, then run the attack over 200 simulated signatures.
exhibits.outcome: Plots modeled timing strata and a round-by-round correlation and distribution estimate; the chosen timing formula creates a leak in leaky mode and flattens it in constant-time mode.
exhibits.limits: No browser clock or physical leakage is measured. The leaky/flat timing formulas predetermine this model's outcome; it does not reproduce the cited hardware power attacks or certify an implementation's side-channel resistance.

exhibits.title: Run Falcon-1024 reference WebAssembly
exhibits.action: Enter a message and click Run real Falcon-1024 on your message.
exhibits.outcome: Loads the falcon-crypto WASM module, generates a keypair, signs and verifies the message, rejects a tampered message, and reports the measured key/signature byte lengths and operation times.
exhibits.limits: Uses the packaged Falcon-1024 reference WASM path only, with its padded signature wrapper; timings vary by device and loading may fail offline or without WebAssembly. It is separate from the page's illustrative signer and toy trapdoor.

exhibits.title: NTRU trapdoor signing versus incomplete-key attempts
exhibits.section: Panel 7 — Real NTRU trapdoor at toy scale (n = 8, Babai round-off)
exhibits.action: Generate an n=8 trapdoor key, sign with its full basis, then try an incomplete basis, a public-key-only forgery and a damaged coefficient of F.
exhibits.outcome: Checks the exact NTRU equation, verifies the full-basis signature against the public key and norm bound, and displays how missing or damaged trapdoor information affects signing attempts.
exhibits.limits: The n=8 lattice offers no security; Babai round-off is an NTRUSign-style teaching mechanism with known leakage, not Falcon's Gaussian sampler or production signer.

exhibits.title: Browser randomness as dice
exhibits.action: Roll five dice several times using the browser random source.
exhibits.outcome: Five faces and the consumed/discarded byte count appear; repeated rolls are compared without treating an accidental repeat as an error.
exhibits.limits: A few rolls do not test or prove entropy quality; the demo relies on crypto.getRandomValues and the host environment.

exhibits.title: Deterministic bytes from a recipe
exhibits.section: Now a computer, following a recipe
exhibits.action: Enter a seed phrase and roll twice without changing it, then alter the phrase and compare.
exhibits.outcome: A SHA-256-derived ChaCha20 generator produces dice and bytes that repeat exactly for the same input.
concepts: cryptographic deterministic random bit generator intuition
exhibits.limits: The seeded generator uses a fixed internal nonce for reproducibility and a guessable input; it is intentionally not a safe key-generation recipe.

exhibits.title: Two keys that look alike
exhibits.section: Step 2 Two keys. Tell them apart.
exhibits.action: Generate a browser-random 32-byte key and a 32-byte ChaCha20-derived key from a four-digit PIN, and inspect both sets of four visual checks.
exhibits.outcome: The two byte strings and simple check results appear side by side; they can both pass despite radically different seed search spaces.
concepts: visual randomness tests cannot prove security
exhibits.limits: Passing these four checks does not establish CSPRNG security. The seeded key is intentionally guessable despite its 256-bit length.

exhibits.title: Checks catch an obvious pattern
exhibits.section: Do those checks do anything at all?
exhibits.action: Run the same four checks on a byte counter.
exhibits.outcome: Failed checks and pattern explanations show what the superficial tests can detect and why passing them proves much less.
exhibits.limits: This is a deliberately obvious nonrandom source and does not validate the sufficiency of the tests for cryptographic use.

exhibits.title: Guess the PIN and recover the seeded key
exhibits.section: Step 3 Guess the seed, take the key
exhibits.action: Try one PIN, then enumerate all 10,000 four-digit PINs against an AES-256-GCM encrypted message made under the seeded key.
exhibits.outcome: AEAD authentication rejects wrong candidate keys; a successful candidate opens the message and reveals the PIN, recovered key and search cost.
exhibits.limits: The full sweep covers exactly four-digit PINs, not every possible seed; the lab does not break ChaCha20, AES-GCM or a well-seeded generator.

exhibits.title: Run the same search against browser randomness
exhibits.action: After making keys, search the same 10,000 candidate PINs against the browser-random key ciphertext and compare with the seeded case.
exhibits.outcome: No candidate opens the browser-random-key message in the expected run; a table contrasts identical cipher, key length and tests with different key origin and observed search result.
concepts: same AES-GCM algorithm different key origins
exhibits.limits: A failed 10,000-PIN search shows only that this key was not found in that candidate set; it does not prove all attacks infeasible or assess host entropy.

exhibits.title: Published and derived cipher checks
exhibits.section: How this demo checks its own results
exhibits.action: Read the on-load vector verdict and optionally expand the individual published and locally derived cases.
exhibits.outcome: ChaCha20 implementation outputs are checked against RFC 8439 vectors and separate changed-input cases, with source provenance and disagreements visible.
exhibits.limits: Passing a finite vector set checks specified cases; it is not a formal proof or security audit of the entire implementation.

exhibits.title: Mosca inequality personal risk calculator
exhibits.section: Personal Risk Calculator — Mosca Inequality for Your Data
exhibits.action: Choose a data type, confidentiality algorithm and CRQC scenario; adjust data lifetime X and migration time Y, or try a preset.
exhibits.outcome: Recalculates the X + Y versus Z planning comparison, algorithm status and a plain-language exposure verdict.
exhibits.limits: Planning model for confidentiality paths, not a CRQC arrival prediction or an observed decryption probability. A vulnerable signature alone cannot decrypt archived ciphertext.

exhibits.title: Year-by-year historical exposure curve
exhibits.action: Select a confidentiality algorithm, toggle four CRQC scenarios, and inspect or download the plotted curve.
exhibits.outcome: Renders an interactive timeline of modelled retrospective decryptability with a crosshair and scenario legend.
exhibits.limits: Uses historical 2024 expert-survey anchors and modelled interpolation rather than the newer 2025 survey; exact values are illustrative, and the AES-128 line is a hypothetical scaling exercise, not a measured AES decryption probability.

exhibits.title: Re-key an archive before toy RSA factoring
exhibits.section: Migration, Executed — What Re-Keying Actually Protects
exhibits.action: Choose an organization, migrate locally held records to AES-256-GCM, then factor the toy RSA modulus and compare records still held with previously captured sessions.
exhibits.outcome: Performs real toy RSA-KEM protection, local re-encryption and Pollard-rho factoring, then reports which ciphertexts the attack can read.
exhibits.limits: The ~64-bit RSA modulus is intentionally factorable by classical Pollard rho; the button's 'CRQC' label is a scenario stand-in, not an implementation of Shor or evidence RSA-2048 is classically broken.

exhibits.title: Run a toy module-LIP public-key recovery
exhibits.action: Choose toy ring degree n=4 or n=8 and click Recover the key from the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Generates a separate toy unimodular basis, publishes Gram matrix Q, builds the tau-cocycle lattice from Q, applies LLL/enumeration and parity filtering, then displays a recovered equivalent basis B′ whose Gram matrix equals Q when successful.
exhibits.limits: Toy n=4/8 reduction on a separate genuinely unimodular toy key, not key recovery on this demo's HAWK-512/1024 keys or a production-scale HAWK key. Plain LLL substitutes for the large-scale shortest-vector procedure.

exhibits.title: Draw from the standalone Gaussian CDT and compare samplers
exhibits.action: Sample both distributions with 4,096 draws each and step through one CDT threshold walk.
exhibits.outcome: Displays measured histogram, theoretical PMF, distribution statistics and elapsed times for table-T1 discrete draws versus a Falcon-style accept/reject comparison; the walk exposes threshold comparisons and sign selection.
exhibits.limits: The T1 table runs here and in the sampler-gap bench, but this build's default signing path substitutes a mod-2 linear solve and does not call T1; the Falcon-style comparison is educational, not a full Falcon implementation or a side-channel certification.

exhibits.title: Sign, verify and forge using the demo's public parity basis
exhibits.action: Choose HAWK-512 or HAWK-1024, enter a message, generate a keypair and sign, then click Forge with only the public key and inspect the unmodified verifier's result.
exhibits.outcome: Computes a lattice signature and public-key verification checks, then derives a second signature from public data alone and reports whether the same verifier accepts it.
exhibits.limits: This educational signing implementation is forgeable by design because it publishes B mod 2 and does not use the production HAWK trapdoor or default Gaussian coset sampler; success of this demo's verifier is not HAWK unforgeability or deployment approval. HAWK was withdrawn in July 2026.

exhibits.title: Measure whether Gaussian sampling fixes the demo forgery
exhibits.action: After generating a keypair, click Measure the sampler gap to compare the mod-2 linear solve with a T1 discrete-Gaussian coset offset on that same key and message.
exhibits.outcome: Reports measured coefficient changes, additivity over integers and mod 2, value diversity, norm inflation and whether public-key-only forgeries under both columns pass the unmodified verifier.
exhibits.limits: The added Gaussian samples the public parity coset using T1, not production HAWK's basis-dependent lattice-coset sampler; it compares this build's exposed-public-basis failure and cannot establish a vulnerability of a correctly implemented HAWK signer.

exhibits.title: Generate an illustrative HQC keypair
exhibits.action: Select HQC-128, -192 or -256 and generate a fresh illustrative sparse-vector keypair.
exhibits.outcome: Computes toy public relation s = x + h·y over a quasi-cyclic bit representation and displays actual sparse supports and public values alongside separately sourced specification sizes.
exhibits.limits: The generated n and private-key representation are illustrative. The published 2026 HQC decapsulation key defaults to a 32-byte seed; this page does not generate production HQC keys.

exhibits.title: Run illustrative HQC encapsulation and decapsulation
exhibits.action: After keygen, run encap and decap and optionally show the intermediate code and Fujisaki–Okamoto steps.
exhibits.outcome: Calculates u, v, d and a shared secret, decodes Reed-Muller/Reed-Solomon layers, reports corrected errors, FO verification and whether Alice/Bob secrets match.
exhibits.limits: Runs an educational reduced-parameter KEM inspired by HQC, not a standard-conformant production HQC encapsulation. Its implicit-rejection fallback differs from the published specification.

exhibits.title: Change ciphertext error placement and measure decoding
exhibits.section: 6. Bit-flip lab — watch the error budget at work
exhibits.action: Adjust the number of flipped ciphertext-v bits and place them anywhere or only in the codeword region; compare decapsulation and FO outcomes.
exhibits.outcome: Counts which flipped bits actually reach the toy decoder, reports Reed-Muller/Reed-Solomon corrections and exact seed recovery, and separately reports FO acceptance.
exhibits.limits: The illustrative decoder has small parameters and its observed correction rate is not a production HQC decapsulation-failure estimate.

exhibits.title: Flip one bit and inspect FO rejection
exhibits.section: 7. Tamper lab — IND-CCA in one click
exhibits.action: Choose u, v or d, enter a bit index, flip it and decapsulate the modified illustrative ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Shows whether the FO tag was accepted and whether the decapsulated secret matches the clean run; a changed ciphertext usually produces a divergent key through implicit rejection.
exhibits.limits: This is a toy behavior demonstration, not an IND-CCA proof. Physical fault attacks on other decapsulation steps are discussed as research context and not executed.

exhibits.title: Measure a secret-indexed lookup timing toy
exhibits.action: Run the browser timing experiment for naive early-return and full-scan lookups at six planted marker positions.
exhibits.outcome: Measures and plots time per lookup on the current device, after verifying each lookup returned the planted index.
exhibits.limits: The code times a JavaScript array toy, not HQC FPGA or real hardware leakage. A full scan in JavaScript does not prove constant-time machine behavior; the 2026 masked-HQC profiling paper is cited context only.

exhibits.title: Compare HQC, BIKE and ML-KEM published sizes
exhibits.action: Choose security level 1, 3 or 5 and inspect the side-by-side KEM table and size bars.
exhibits.outcome: Displays published key/ciphertext/shared-secret sizes and historical cycle figures with assumption and failure-rate context.
exhibits.limits: HQC numbers are taken from its 12 October 2026 team specification, not a final NIST FIPS; BIKE and ML-KEM use other sources. Historical cycle counts come from different platforms and are not a controlled performance comparison.

exhibits.title: Step through a classical and post-quantum handshake
exhibits.action: Use Next, Prev, or Reset to inspect X25519 key exchange, ML-KEM-768 encapsulation/decapsulation, and the HKDF combiner.
exhibits.outcome: The browser computes both shared secrets, derives matching 32-byte session keys and shows the separate wires and combiner inputs as the six steps unfold.
exhibits.limits: The browser's X25519-secret-first HKDF construction is a teaching exchange, not the TLS X25519MLKEM768 wire format or transcript-bound key schedule (demos/hybrid-wire/src/main.ts:410).

exhibits.title: Test one-wire and two-wire compromise
exhibits.action: Toggle recovered X25519 and ML-KEM secrets separately or together and inspect the attacker's candidate derivations and intercepted-record decryption.
exhibits.outcome: The attack runs the actual HKDF combiner with known or guessed inputs: one hidden secret prevents the tested candidates from opening the record; revealing both yields the session key and opens it.
exhibits.limits: The toggle assumes a complete 32-byte secret has been recovered; eight random guesses against a hidden secret illustrate the condition rather than prove every real-world deployment secure.

exhibits.title: Tamper with a hybrid session
exhibits.action: After completing the handshake, send a message and flip a byte in the ML-KEM ciphertext via Tamper with session; try recipient decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Bob derives a different session key and AES-GCM authentication rejects the resulting message.
exhibits.limits: The demo models a browser teaching exchange rather than a full authenticated TLS handshake.

exhibits.title: HKDF: Extract and Expand
exhibits.action: Change input key material, salt, context info and output length, then derive.
exhibits.outcome: Show computed PRK, OKM, expansion blocks and a two-phase diagram populated with the actual derived bytes.
exhibits.limits: HKDF expects high-entropy input key material; it is not a password-stretching function.

exhibits.title: Argon2id: Modern Password Hashing
exhibits.action: Set password, salt, time, memory, parallelism and tag length, then derive an Argon2id output.
exhibits.outcome: Read the output, browser runtime, selected memory cost and estimated password-guessing attack cost.
exhibits.limits: Browser timing and attacker-cost estimates are illustrative; memory-hardness does not guarantee a side-channel-free implementation or make GPU and ASIC attacks impossible.

exhibits.title: Stretch then Fan Out
exhibits.action: Supply one password and salt, edit three context strings, then run Argon2id followed by HKDF expansion.
exhibits.outcome: See one derived root and separately labelled context-specific output keys in a fan-out diagram, including the total runtime.
exhibits.limits: A teaching composition with fixed Argon2id parameters; this does not model a whole TLS, Signal or vault key schedule.
exhibits.section: The KDF Chain: Stretch then Fan Out

exhibits.title: PBKDF2 Password Stretching
exhibits.action: Set password, salt, iterations and length; derive or benchmark 100k, 600k and 1M iterations.
exhibits.outcome: Compare HMAC-SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-512 output and measured browser time plus an attack-cost estimate.
exhibits.limits: Browser benchmark measures this device; offline-attack cost is an estimate. PBKDF2 is CPU-hard, not memory-hard.

exhibits.title: scrypt Memory-Hard Stretching
exhibits.action: Adjust N, r, p, salt and password; derive a key or compare three N values.
exhibits.outcome: See output bytes, measured runtime and estimated memory consumption; very large settings may exceed browser memory.
exhibits.limits: Benchmarks depend on the device and may fail under browser memory limits; they do not directly measure GPU attack throughput.

exhibits.title: Why Memory Hardness Beats GPUs
exhibits.action: Move among labelled memory-cost settings and animate the access grid.
exhibits.outcome: See a teaching visualization where a one-MiB cell scale and waiting cores illustrate greater per-guess memory demand.
exhibits.limits: A single-bus visualization, not an instrumented GPU trace or measured attack cost.

exhibits.title: Key lifecycle decisions
exhibits.section: Follow the key, from creation to retirement
exhibits.action: Choose between two decisions at each of ten stages and move through the path.
exhibits.outcome: Feedback explains generation, binding, purpose separation, rotation, custody, recovery, compromise, lifetimes, destruction and public-key trust.
exhibits.limits: Policy scenarios only; choices do not perform transfer, backup, revocation, sanitization or public-key verification.

exhibits.title: Historical key compromise
exhibits.action: Encrypt records, rotate to B, copy old Key A, and run attacker decryption.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto AES-256-GCM ciphertext remains under A after rotation; independent captured A decrypts an archived record and validates its tag.
exhibits.limits: Fictional records and simulated custody incident; real browser cryptography does not model production key service or persistent storage.

exhibits.title: Re-encryption and key retirement
exhibits.action: Re-encrypt remaining library records under B, discard the library’s A reference, and compare readability with the attacker’s archived copy.
exhibits.outcome: Current record epochs change while a captured A ciphertext remains exposed; discarding A may make remaining old records unreadable.
exhibits.limits: Deleting a JavaScript CryptoKey reference is not secure erasure of all copies or backups.

exhibits.title: Authenticated encryption tampering
exhibits.action: After encrypting, press Try tampering.
exhibits.outcome: A modified ciphertext byte is rejected by WebCrypto AES-GCM; this check does not reveal key theft.
exhibits.limits: Only one deliberate byte flip; successful authentication of an unmodified record says nothing about key custody.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM stepper
exhibits.action: Select ML-KEM-512, 768, or 1024 and advance KeyGen, Encaps, and Decaps.
exhibits.outcome: Displays generated artifacts, operation timings, and a byte-for-byte match of both parties' 32-byte shared secrets.
exhibits.limits: Local browser library is not a FIPS-validated module and the flow has no peer authentication; final FIPS 203 ML-KEM is not byte compatible with every pre-standard Kyber protocol.

exhibits.title: Full hybrid encryption (ML-KEM + AES-256-GCM)
exhibits.action: Enter plaintext, encrypt and decrypt it, then flip a byte of the ML-KEM ciphertext and try decryption again.
exhibits.outcome: Runs ML-KEM encapsulation, HKDF-SHA256, and AES-256-GCM; shows authentication/decryption result or failure after tampering.
exhibits.limits: Teaching-only encryption path lacks peer authentication and independent audit. ML-KEM ciphertext modification by itself may yield a different decapsulated secret; GCM then rejects the derived-key mismatch.

exhibits.title: Learning With Errors: the noise is the whole point
exhibits.section: Learning With Errors: the noise is the whole point
exhibits.action: Generate a tiny q=17 scalar LWE instance; solve its clean and noisy equations by Gaussian elimination and count toy candidates.
exhibits.outcome: Shows when exact linear algebra recovers the secret from clean equations and how noise usually changes that result.
exhibits.limits: 4x4 scalar toy with Math.random; it is intentionally searchable, sometimes singular, and does not implement ML-KEM's module lattice or estimate its security.

exhibits.title: Cyclic NTT polynomial multiplication
exhibits.action: Run an eight-point cyclic NTT on two small polynomials, step butterflies, and compare the inverse result with schoolbook multiplication.
exhibits.outcome: Displays NTT, pointwise product, inverse transform, butterfly trace, and a match or mismatch verdict for the toy cyclic ring.
exhibits.limits: Computes Z_3329[X]/(X^8-1), not FIPS 203's incomplete negacyclic ML-KEM NTT or its base-case multiplication.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM parameter sets and fresh key-establishment wire cost
exhibits.action: Compare FIPS 203 key and ciphertext sizes and select a profile to use in the real ML-KEM stepper.
exhibits.outcome: Shows parameter categories and construction-level bytes for X25519, ML-KEM-512/768/1024, and X25519 plus ML-KEM-768.
exhibits.limits: Static construction-level payload accounting excludes certificates, signatures, framing, retransmissions and protocol-specific key caching; categories are not exact bit-strength values.

exhibits.title: Browser benchmark
exhibits.action: Run warm-up and repeated ML-KEM KeyGen/Encaps/Decaps timings and optional native X25519 timings; export JSON or CSV samples.
exhibits.outcome: Shows local median and p95 timing, environment metadata and raw sample exports.
exhibits.limits: Pure-JavaScript ML-KEM and native Web Crypto X25519 backends differ; these local wall-clock timings are not portable rankings or side-channel measurements. X25519 result may be unavailable in a browser.

exhibits.title: Break the toy cipher
exhibits.action: Choose known-plaintext traffic, rounds, S-box, final-key nibble and approximation; run the attack or use starvation, added-round, and bad-relation presets.
exhibits.outcome: Sixteen candidate counters rank a guessed four-bit last-round subkey with success/failure verdict and screening context.
exhibits.limits: Only an 8-bit toy SPN and a four-bit subkey nibble are attacked; a successful run is not a modern cipher break.

exhibits.title: Inspect the cipher
exhibits.action: Slide an eight-bit plaintext value through the selected SPN.
exhibits.outcome: The encryption walkthrough updates and highlights the pre-final-round state that a nibble guess can partially undo.
exhibits.limits: Eight-bit classroom cipher; the walkthrough is not DES or AES.

exhibits.title: Inspect one S-box leak
exhibits.action: Select an input-mask/output-mask cell in the 16×16 linear approximation table.
exhibits.outcome: A detail view enumerates all sixteen S-box inputs and shows agreement counts and bias for the selected parity equation.
exhibits.limits: The statistics are exact for a four-bit teaching S-box; LAT cells are not direct attack success probabilities.

exhibits.title: Watch the bias compound
exhibits.action: Apply trail rounds one at a time and open the measured-versus-predicted bias detail.
exhibits.outcome: Per-round correlations and predicted aggregate bias shrink; a full-codebook measurement across keys exposes linear-hull reinforcement or cancellation.
exhibits.limits: The lemma assumes independent approximations; real whole-cipher bias can differ, as the panel itself measures.

exhibits.title: How much traffic do you need?
exhibits.action: Run complete attacks over sixty toy keys at several sample sizes, then compare repeated versus distinct known-plaintext sampling.
exhibits.outcome: Tables juxtapose the inverse-square single-counter prediction with measured key-ranking success, duplicate-input counts, Wilson intervals, and finite-population correction.
exhibits.limits: Measurements are over random keys of an 8-bit toy cipher; intervals describe across-key proportions, not guarantees for a key or a real cipher.
exhibits.section: How much traffic do you need?

exhibits.title: The pair-mate attack
exhibits.action: Read the comparison table of differential and linear cryptanalysis on the same toy SPN.
exhibits.outcome: The page contrasts attack access, measured relation and target information for the two cryptanalytic methods.
exhibits.limits: The comparison is explanatory; this section does not run a differential attack.

exhibits.title: Scramble a toy binary Goppa generator
exhibits.section: 1. Binary Goppa Codes and the McEliece Trapdoor
exhibits.action: Switch between Bob's structured generator G, the row-mixed S·G matrix, and the permuted public Gpub matrix.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the computed toy matrices and explanatory captions showing how obvious visual structure changes under row mixing and column permutation.
exhibits.limits: A GF(16), n=16 toy visual; a random-looking matrix display does not establish indistinguishability or structural-attack resistance of real Classic McEliece keys.

exhibits.title: Toy Goppa encapsulation, Patterson decoding and tampering
exhibits.action: Encapsulate, toggle ciphertext bits or exceed the correction radius, decapsulate with the trapdoor, and run the toy brute-force attacker comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the ciphertext and error weight, Patterson decoding steps and success or failure, shared-secret agreement, and the toy attack's search result; successful decapsulation can key an AES-GCM message round-trip.
exhibits.limits: A n=16, t=2 teaching KEM with toy brute force, not the production Classic McEliece KEM, a practical attack on real parameters, or the 2026 structural preprint's recovery method.

exhibits.title: Step the modular entropy multiplier
exhibits.section: The modular entropy multiplier, one step at a time
exhibits.action: Press Step the circuit, Step 8 times, or Reset.
exhibits.outcome: The analog-state marker moves through threshold, fold/stretch rule and emitted bit strip; a deterministic seeded model makes adjacent-bit dependence visible.
exhibits.limits: Transcribed simulation from vendor circuit; no connected physical device, and its design rate is not a measured entropy estimate.

exhibits.title: Design rate and assessed estimate
exhibits.section: A design rate is not a measurement
exhibits.action: Compare the device design log2(K) rate with the pinned assessment and driver ceiling.
exhibits.outcome: Separately labeled theoretical and native-tool-on-model figures expose the gap.
exhibits.limits: Native assessment concerns one model-generated million-sample file, not a hardware certification or live calculation.

exhibits.title: Inspect sample bytes
exhibits.action: Select a shipped fixture or local file, choose layout and symbol width, then Analyse.
exhibits.outcome: Worker computes balance, runs, repeated blocks, lag autocorrelation and byte/bit previews.
exhibits.limits: Descriptive statistics are not SP 800-90B entropy estimates; uploaded files stay local and have an input cap.

exhibits.title: Pinned non-IID assessment
exhibits.action: Select a shipped fixture and inspect the minimum, per-bit conversion, branch rule and individual non-IID estimators.
exhibits.outcome: Recorded native SP 800-90B assessment shows the binding estimator and distinctions among bits per sample and bits per bit; custom files show Not Run.
exhibits.limits: No browser estimator for changed/uploaded bytes; a figure applies only to its exact hashed fixture and recorded native run.

exhibits.title: Compare two assessment implementations
exhibits.action: Select one of seven published synthetic inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Pinned NIST-fork and Theseus values for ten estimators, absolute differences and overall minima are displayed with input hashes.
exhibits.limits: Recorded native runs only; six synthetic model seeds are not a confidence interval or hardware entropy claim.

exhibits.title: IID assumption decision
exhibits.action: Select a specified source scenario and reveal the explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that bias can coexist with IID, while memory, drift, and a public alternating rule defeat inferences from balanced histograms.
exhibits.limits: Specified thought-experiment models; the answer is not inferred from a finite statistical test.

exhibits.title: Faults versus reported estimate
exhibits.section: What the faults did to the reported figure
exhibits.action: Compare clean and deliberately faulty model fixtures and inspect estimator-by-estimator differences.
exhibits.outcome: Some faults raise the reported minimum despite other estimators dropping; pinned native results and fixture provenance are shown.
exhibits.limits: Precomputed model fixtures; the browser does not reassess edited/custom files.

exhibits.title: Reproduce predictable counter-hash
exhibits.section: The experiment: a stream everyone can predict
exhibits.action: Regenerate the first 64 bytes from the published SHA-256 counter construction.
exhibits.outcome: Regenerated bytes match a predictable fixture whose pinned assessment looks high, demonstrating sample statistics cannot prove unknown source entropy.
exhibits.limits: SHA-256 computation is real; the high assessment is a pinned native result on a published deterministic file, not a genuine secret entropy claim.

exhibits.title: Output multiplier entropy ledger
exhibits.section: The driver’s sponge, and its output multiplier
exhibits.action: Move outputMultiplier slider and inspect output bits versus fixed input entropy budget and sponge output.
exhibits.outcome: More output bytes dilute the chargeable entropy per output bit while the input budget bar stays fixed.
exhibits.limits: Ledger uses a design/driver ceiling rather than measuring raw hardware entropy; initial sponge input may be a labeled placeholder until model bytes load.

exhibits.title: Before and after conditioning
exhibits.section: The same source, measured before and after conditioning
exhibits.action: Compare pinned raw and conditioned fixture assessments.
exhibits.outcome: The measured per-output-bit number rises after conditioning although the modeled source did not gain entropy.
exhibits.limits: Pinned native measurements of model-generated streams; a high conditioned-output figure cannot establish source entropy.

exhibits.title: Public pad decryption
exhibits.section: A public pad is not a pad
exhibits.action: Enter a message and pad length, then Encrypt, then decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Real SHA-256-generated public pad and XOR ciphertext recover the message without a secret; short pad reveals an uncovered tail.
exhibits.limits: The pad construction is deliberately public and predictable; this is an insecurity demonstration, not secure OTP use.

exhibits.title: Two-time-pad XOR leak
exhibits.section: Used twice, the pad cancels itself
exhibits.action: Enter two messages and reuse the same pad once.
exhibits.outcome: The two ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of the plaintext prefixes, with the pad canceling.
exhibits.limits: Demo uses a public deterministic pad and the common length prefix; the algebraic cancellation holds for any reused XOR pad.

exhibits.title: The XOR reveal
exhibits.action: Encrypt two editable messages under one key and reused nonce, then enter and slide a guessed crib.
exhibits.outcome: See C1 XOR C2 equal P1 XOR P2 and recover matching bytes of the second message without the encryption key.
exhibits.limits: The learner can see and edit both teaching plaintexts; a real attacker needs an accurate guess about one message.
exhibits.section: The XOR reveal — recover a message you were never given

exhibits.title: Same mistake, four outcomes
exhibits.action: Run fresh-versus-reused IV/nonce scenarios for AES-CTR, AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-CBC.
exhibits.outcome: Read primitive return values separately from security verdicts and a running table of plaintext exposure, forgery and key recovery; CBC reuse reveals prefix equality while AEAD reuse enables nonce-specific forgery.
exhibits.limits: The scoreboard records the demonstrated scenario and explicitly does not claim recovery of the AES or ChaCha20 encryption key; CBC and CTR supply no authentication.

exhibits.title: CBC: different IVs can still leak
exhibits.action: Run the chosen-plaintext predictable-IV case against a control where plaintext is committed before a fresh IV is drawn.
exhibits.outcome: Observe identical first ciphertext blocks under distinct, predictable IVs when P2=P1 XOR IV1 XOR IV2, compared with the random-IV control.
exhibits.limits: Controlled first-block equality only; no AES key or unknown-plaintext recovery, and no claim of a CBC padding oracle.
exhibits.section: CBC: different IVs can still leak

exhibits.title: One-time pad: encrypt and decrypt
exhibits.action: Type a message or generate a new random key of equal UTF-8 byte length.
exhibits.outcome: Byte strips display P, K, P XOR K, and exact recovery by ciphertext XOR K.
concepts: key length equals message byte length
exhibits.limits: Correct use requires a secret uniformly random key shared out of band and never reused; key distribution is not modeled.

exhibits.title: Perfect secrecy: every plaintext is possible
exhibits.action: Enter any plaintext with the fixed ciphertext's exact byte length.
exhibits.outcome: The UI derives K=C XOR P and verifies that the same ciphertext decrypts to the chosen plaintext under that key.
exhibits.limits: The algebra shows possible keys; the secrecy guarantee also needs a uniformly random one-use secret pad.
exhibits.section: 2 · Perfect secrecy — every plaintext is possible

exhibits.title: Limits of perfect secrecy
exhibits.action: Shorten an eight-bit pad, inspect all 256 one-byte candidates, compute an exact two-message indistinguishability game, and edit a four-key encryption table.
exhibits.outcome: The grid rules out unreachable messages, exact fractions show an attacker's success, and independent Shannon-condition checks agree or fail for the editable table.
exhibits.limits: These are tiny exhaustive finite spaces, not measured security of a deployed cipher.

exhibits.title: Prior odds and what a ciphertext changes
exhibits.action: Adjust four prior message weights and select a two-bit observed ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: An exact prior/posterior table contrasts fresh uniform pad, fresh biased pad, and known-plaintext pad reuse.
exhibits.limits: Two-bit exact teaching models; the reuse column is a separate two-encryption known-plaintext attack, not the outcome of a single ciphertext.
exhibits.section: D · Prior odds and what a ciphertext changes

exhibits.title: Two-time pad: key reuse and crib dragging
exhibits.action: Edit two messages, toggle one reused key versus independent fresh keys, drag or nudge a guessed crib, and pin candidates.
exhibits.outcome: With reuse, C1 XOR C2 reveals P1 XOR P2 and the crib workbench reconstructs overlapping bytes in both plaintexts; with separate keys, the cancellation disappears.
exhibits.limits: The XOR attack covers only overlapping keystream bytes; guesses require plausible plaintext context.
exhibits.section: 3 · Two-time pad — the catastrophic key-reuse attack

exhibits.title: Keystream reuse in real ciphers: structural analogy
exhibits.action: Edit two messages encrypted with the same generated stand-in keystream and crib-drag the XOR strip.
exhibits.outcome: The shared keystream cancels, exposing the same P1 XOR P2 reconstruction pattern as the two-time pad.
exhibits.limits: The page does not run ChaCha20, AES-CTR, or AES-GCM; GCM authentication consequences are not demonstrated.
exhibits.section: 4 · Keystream reuse in real ciphers — the same break

exhibits.title: Import two ciphertexts: cryptanalysis playground
exhibits.action: Paste two hex ciphertexts or load a challenge, then slide and pin cribs in the shared workbench.
exhibits.outcome: The overlapping ciphertext XOR strip and candidate plaintext bytes appear; bundled challenges permit an optional instructor reveal.
exhibits.limits: The method helps recover plaintext only when the inputs share keystream bytes; it does not recover a general encryption key.

exhibits.title: Generate a Paillier keypair
exhibits.action: Choose a 64–192-bit educational modulus size and generate a keypair in a worker; inspect N, g and the private parameters.
exhibits.outcome: The page computes primes and Paillier key material and displays the resulting modulus bit length, which can be one bit below the nominal selection.
exhibits.limits: These tiny sizes are deliberately factorable and unsuitable for deployment; the page does not model a hardened key generator.

exhibits.title: Factor the educational modulus
exhibits.action: Press Factor N against the generated small modulus and watch a budgeted Pollard rho search.
exhibits.outcome: When factoring succeeds within the budget, the worker reports steps/time, rebuilds the private key and can decrypt a ciphertext made in the preceding section; larger attempts may give up.
exhibits.limits: Success is conditional on tiny educational keys and a fixed search budget; it is not a practical attack on properly sized Paillier.

exhibits.title: Encrypt, repeat and re-randomize a message
exhibits.action: Encrypt a number, encrypt it again with fresh randomness, decrypt the ciphertext, then re-randomize it using only the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Different ciphertexts can decrypt to the same number; the page shows the new ciphertext and the decryption of each stored example.
exhibits.limits: The demonstration uses very small, insecure key sizes; a re-randomization can occasionally return an unchanged ciphertext when the fresh factor is one.

exhibits.title: Multiply ciphertexts to add plaintexts
exhibits.action: Encrypt two inputs or hand in earlier ciphertexts, multiply the ciphertexts modulo N², decrypt the product, and try the modulus-overflow preset.
exhibits.outcome: The product decrypts to (A+B) mod N; the page also actually decrypts a naive integer sum of ciphertexts to show it generally fails and exposes wraparound when A+B reaches N.
exhibits.limits: The plain sum must be kept below N to represent the intended integer; Paillier alone does not authenticate ciphertexts.

exhibits.title: Aggregate encrypted counts with public weights
exhibits.action: Enter counts and optional weights, then aggregate encrypted counts and exponentiate ciphertexts by public weights.
exhibits.outcome: The page decrypts the encrypted sum and weighted sum and compares them with plaintext totals, showing each encrypted weighted contribution.
exhibits.limits: The scenario uses one local decryption key and educational modulus sizes; it is not a distributed private analytics protocol.

exhibits.title: Rewrite an encrypted ballot and compare MAC admission
exhibits.action: Seal a set of 0/1 ballots, select a ballot and a public-key vote boost, then forge and re-tally with the Encrypt-then-MAC check on or off.
exhibits.outcome: Without authentication the forged ciphertext changes the tally despite hiding the original vote; with the MAC check the altered ballot is rejected, and the page shows the effect of dropping it.
exhibits.limits: This locally keyed MAC checks outsider tampering, not whether an authorized voter submitted a valid 0-or-1 plaintext; it is not a full election protocol.

exhibits.title: Four classical PAKE handshakes
exhibits.action: Run Honest run, Wrong password, or Step one message in SRP-6a, then Go deeper to unlock J-PAKE, CPace and Dragonfly.
exhibits.outcome: Peer scratchpads and wire messages show derived session-key fingerprints; matching confirmed keys turn green, wrong-password handshakes fail.
exhibits.limits: Hand-rolled educational browser engines are not constant-time or production authentication; all four runnable engines are classical.

exhibits.title: Register SRP verifier
exhibits.action: Type a throwaway password and Register {salt, v}, then run the SRP handshake.
exhibits.outcome: Server stores a salt and derived verifier while the demo shows the password staying in the client scratchpad.
exhibits.limits: Demo inputs are shown on screen; do not enter real credentials; an SRP verifier can enable offline guessing after breach.

exhibits.title: Stolen SRP verifier dictionary attack
exhibits.action: After a handshake, open Server breach and run the offline grind with optional candidate guesses.
exhibits.outcome: Real modular exponentiation recomputes verifiers and reports a match if the password is in the tested list; passive transcript scan is shown separately.
exhibits.limits: Finite browser wordlist and local throughput are not a GPU benchmark; literal transcript scan is not a proof of PAKE security.

exhibits.title: On-path transcript inspection
exhibits.action: Open On-path observer after a handshake and inspect raw wire fields and literal-encoding audit.
exhibits.outcome: The visible transcript contains public fields and no recognized literal password encoding in the scanned forms.
exhibits.limits: Scanning strings for literal password encodings is a backstop, not proof that no offline password test exists.

exhibits.title: Curated message tampering
exhibits.action: Go deeper, choose a curated wire-field modification, and run the exchange.
exhibits.outcome: The receiving engine aborts or confirmation fails at the affected step, with a visible reason.
exhibits.limits: Curated single-field mutations only; not a comprehensive adversarial security proof.

exhibits.title: Dragonfly iteration-count leak
exhibits.action: Choose password candidates in the legacy versus fixed-work graph.
exhibits.outcome: Modeled hunting-and-pecking iteration counts vary for legacy early exit and flatten under the fixed-work teaching variant.
exhibits.limits: Modeled iteration count, not measured browser timing; flat count addresses one historical signal, not cache/branch/field-arithmetic leakage or modern SAE hash-to-element.

exhibits.title: PAKE family property matrix
exhibits.action: Compare rows for balanced versus augmented server storage, rounds, construction and standardization.
exhibits.outcome: Matrix places runnable classical families and reference-only OPAQUE side by side with status and deployment context.
exhibits.limits: Reference rows are not runnable implementations; status is sourced from data table and may change over time.

exhibits.title: Post-quantum PAKE boundary
exhibits.action: Read the architecture note and source links.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that runnable group-based PAKE engines are classical and that KEM/password encoding extension remains unimplemented.
exhibits.limits: No post-quantum PAKE engine is implemented; model-conditional preprint discussion does not establish a practical break of the classical demos.

exhibits.title: The Chain
exhibits.action: Select the root, intermediate, or leaf certificate.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect subject, issuer, validity, key and signature details and see which private key signs which certificate.
exhibits.limits: JSON-serialized teaching certificates with WebCrypto signatures, not ASN.1/DER X.509 or complete RFC 5280 path validation.

exhibits.title: Chain Validation and Revocation Evidence
exhibits.action: Run validation; tamper a node, choose missing/current/stale/wrong-signer OCSP evidence, and switch revocation policy.
exhibits.outcome: Read per-link signature checks and an overall trust verdict; a signed but stale good response or missing evidence changes the policy decision without changing certificate signatures.
exhibits.limits: OCSP is directly issuer-signed JSON in this toy; no OCSP wire protocol or complete TLS revocation policy.

exhibits.title: Trust Stores
exhibits.action: Switch among Browser, OS and Application store tabs.
exhibits.outcome: Compare accepted and rejected verdicts for the same signed chain depending on whether its root is a chosen trust anchor.
exhibits.limits: Illustrative in-memory stores, not queries to the visitor's actual browser or operating-system trust store.

exhibits.title: Certificate Transparency
exhibits.action: Submit certificate entries, request inclusion and consistency proofs, select a tree leaf, or simulate misissuance.
exhibits.outcome: See the Merkle tree, SCT entry, proof verification status and misissuance monitor; proof readouts are invalidated when the log grows.
exhibits.limits: A browser-local simulated CT log and monitor; inclusion makes issuance visible but does not prove it was authorized or revoke a certificate.

exhibits.title: CA Compromise
exhibits.action: Select an uncompromised, intermediate-compromised or root-compromised scenario.
exhibits.outcome: Observe a distrusted subtree and the distinction between still-valid signatures and policy distrust.
exhibits.limits: A selected compromise flag models trust policy; it does not actually steal a CA key or issue a real certificate.

exhibits.title: PQ Migration
exhibits.action: Switch among P-256, ML-DSA and hybrid signature footprint tabs.
exhibits.outcome: Compare live-chain P-256 signature size with FIPS 204 reference ML-DSA sizes and a hybrid estimate.
exhibits.limits: Only P-256 is measured live; ML-DSA is a published reference size, not a generated browser signature; no hybrid certificate is constructed.

exhibits.title: Correlation Power Analysis: recover an AES key byte
exhibits.section: Break it yourself: pull an AES key byte out of the noise
exhibits.action: Change the trace-count and noise sliders, choose a reproducible seed, and run the key-byte correlation attack.
exhibits.outcome: Plots the correlation scores for 256 key-byte guesses, the true byte's rank, and whether the simulated leakage lets the attack recover byte 0; can freeze and export the result.
exhibits.limits: The AES and correlation are computed, but power traces are generated by a model; this is not a measured attack on a chip or on browser timing.

exhibits.title: First-order CPA against masking, shuffling, and hiding
exhibits.section: Defended, defeated, or just more expensive?
exhibits.action: Select none, Boolean masking, shuffling, or added noise and click Attack the defended chip.
exhibits.outcome: Regenerates 4,000 simulated traces, reruns the same CPA, and shows a rank and verdict for the chosen defense.
exhibits.limits: The masking result concerns this first-order leakage model and first-order CPA only; the page names but does not implement a second-order attack or prove hardware resistance.

exhibits.title: Hypothetical AES table-lookup cache-line leak
exhibits.section: What a table lookup can reveal through a cache line
exhibits.action: Enter a known plaintext byte and compare a secret-indexed table lookup with uniform access across all cache lines.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights the idealized observed lines and reports the number of key-byte guesses consistent with each observation.
exhibits.limits: A one-byte perfect-observation model with a hypothetical T-table and 64-byte lines; no cache timing is measured, and the lab's JavaScript AES uses a different S-box layout.

exhibits.title: Explore five post-quantum families
exhibits.action: Select lattice, code, hash, multivariate or isogeny family, then switch between overview, math, notable cryptanalysis and primary-source tabs.
exhibits.outcome: The page displays sourced representative schemes, status, assumptions, tradeoffs and dated research summaries; it warns when an individual scheme was broken rather than declaring an entire family broken.
exhibits.limits: This explorer displays authored research/status summaries. It does not execute cryptanalysis, test all schemes, or turn its heuristic standardisation confidence score into a measured security quantity.

exhibits.title: Compare sizes across families
exhibits.action: Switch between public-key, secret-key, and ciphertext/signature metrics for representative parameter sets.
exhibits.outcome: Plots source-data byte counts on a log2 scale, making relative size tradeoffs visible.
exhibits.limits: Bars are representative parameter values and some entries approximate; verify any deployment selection against the named scheme specification. No key pair or ciphertext is generated by this chart.

exhibits.title: Calculate textbook information-set decoding work
exhibits.section: ISD Work: Prange Attack Cost for Code Parameters
exhibits.action: Use Classic McEliece presets or change code length n, dimension k, and error weight t.
exhibits.outcome: Recomputes Prange success probability and expected log2 work using binomial ratios, plus an illustrative half-exponent quantum scaling and category-floor comparison.
exhibits.limits: This computes a textbook cost formula, not a real key-recovery attack or an overall scheme security estimate. Modern ISD, memory tradeoffs and structural attacks are not modeled.

exhibits.title: Generate and verify a Lamport one-time signature
exhibits.action: Generate a 256-bit-width Lamport keypair, sign a chosen message, verify it, then edit the message and verify again.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto SHA-256 commitments produce a real one-time signature; the page shows which private halves are revealed and rejects a signature after message tampering.
exhibits.limits: This is a plain one-time Lamport scheme, not an implementation of standardized SLH-DSA, XMSS or LMS.

exhibits.title: Reuse a Lamport key and forge at toy digest width
exhibits.section: Now actually forge one — at a toy width
exhibits.action: Sign a second message under the same key to inspect leaked secret halves; choose a 12-, 16-, or 20-bit toy digest and run a covered-message forgery.
exhibits.outcome: The browser derives key material from two observed signatures, searches SHA-256 candidates at the truncated width, and feeds a forged signature to the same verifier, with a negative control for an uncovered message.
exhibits.limits: The successful forgery is deliberately restricted to 12–20 digest bits; the full-width two-signature forgery grind remains out of reach in this browser lab. It is not a break of SLH-DSA.

exhibits.title: Full Handshake, Live
exhibits.action: Step or auto-play through the client and server exchange; Reset generates fresh values.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the serialized hybrid ClientHello and ServerHello, independently computed 64-byte ML-KEM-768 || X25519 secrets, and their match result.
exhibits.limits: Both TLS peers run inside the browser; this is an educational simulation of hello exchange and key schedule, not a production TLS stack or a network TLS connection.

exhibits.title: Why Hybrid?
exhibits.action: Read the threat scenarios and which component still protects the connection.
exhibits.outcome: A static table shows the intended hedge if one component's security assumption fails; no attacker or downgrade is executed.
exhibits.limits: Static threat scenarios are simplified conditional claims, not a tested security proof or a demonstration of Shor's algorithm.

exhibits.title: Building the Hybrid Secret
exhibits.action: Inspect the per-run ML-KEM and X25519 secret previews and press Reset to regenerate the exchange.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ML-KEM || X25519 in RFC 10024 order entering the TLS 1.3 HKDF key schedule, with actual handshake and traffic secret previews.
exhibits.limits: The previews come from real local computations; no finished TLS record protection or remote peer is shown.

exhibits.title: Size and Compute Impact
exhibits.action: Compare the current hybrid and classical hello sizes and locally timed key exchange operations; Reset refreshes the measurement.
exhibits.outcome: Shows measured byte counts, best-of-samples CPU timings and an approximate 1500-byte MTU visual.
exhibits.limits: CPU measurements are local microbenchmarks, not network latency or portable performance rankings. The MTU graphic uses a typical boundary; it does not simulate packets or middleboxes.

exhibits.title: Wire Format Inspector
exhibits.action: Enable Show wire bytes and select the named group, X25519, or ML-KEM byte region.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights computed offsets in the actual serialized ClientHello generated by the local exchange, eliding the large middle of the ML-KEM share.
exhibits.limits: Inspector shows a locally serialized teaching ClientHello, not packets captured from a live TLS connection.

exhibits.title: Deployment Reality
exhibits.action: Read the dated deployment note and the linked IETF group identifier.
exhibits.outcome: Displays adoption context and a source link for RFC 10024's X25519MLKEM768 group 0x11EC.
exhibits.limits: Adoption figure is explicitly dated mid-September 2025; this panel measures no live deployment.

exhibits.title: Build a PQXDH transcript
exhibits.action: Step through Bob's signed prekey bundle, Alice's four X25519 Diffie-Hellman terms and ML-KEM encapsulation, initial-message delivery, and independent Bob derivation.
exhibits.outcome: The browser computes five secret components and an HKDF-SHA-512 session key, measures wire fields, verifies the AES-GCM initial message, and compares Alice's and Bob's keys byte for byte.
exhibits.limits: This is a browser teaching profile of Signal's PQXDH Revision 3, using separate strict Ed25519 signatures and standardized ML-KEM-1024 in place of the revision's XEdDSA and Kyber example. It is not wire-compatible with libsignal; no quantum algorithm runs here.

exhibits.title: Grant curve and lattice breaks to an adversary model
exhibits.section: Open the boxes the model grants
exhibits.action: Complete the handshake, grant the model all X25519 private keys with Curve break, then optionally grant it the ML-KEM secret with Lattice break.
exhibits.outcome: With only the curve grant, it recomputes four DH outputs but lacks the KEM secret and cannot rederive the session key; with both grants, it derives the same session key.
exhibits.limits: The model directly hands private values to the adversary. It neither runs Shor's algorithm nor breaks ML-KEM, and does not prove the security of a deployed implementation.

exhibits.title: Corrupt a prekey signature or ML-KEM ciphertext
exhibits.action: Run the prekey-signature corruption and KEM ciphertext-bit-flip controls on fresh handshakes.
exhibits.outcome: Alice aborts on a bad PQ prekey signature before the handshake; after KEM ciphertext tampering, Bob's first AES-GCM authentication rejects the message.
exhibits.limits: These controlled failure cases are not a chosen-ciphertext security proof or exhaustive malformed-input analysis.

exhibits.title: Exhaust one-time PQ prekeys
exhibits.action: Enable Reuse last-resort key and run two Alice handshakes against the same fallback public key.
exhibits.outcome: The panel checks that the same last-resort PQ prekey identifier served both sessions while their encapsulated shared secrets differ.
exhibits.limits: Reusing the fallback public key does not by itself reveal either session key; the page conditions future compromise on recovering the retained private key and other needed inputs.

exhibits.title: Test authentication and post-compromise healing limits
exhibits.section: Two green handshakes, two missing guarantees
exhibits.action: Substitute a signed bundle under granted classical identity secrets, then compromise and ratchet a completed session with Curve break on or off.
exhibits.outcome: The first model confirms a valid classical signature can accompany adversary control of the initial message; the reduced X25519 ratchet refreshes roots for honest peers, but a curve-break grant can let the adversary follow those roots.
exhibits.limits: This reduced DH-root update is not full Double Ratchet, SPQR or Triple Ratchet; the adversary is explicitly granted secrets rather than running a quantum recovery algorithm.

exhibits.title: Private VOPRF token issuance and redemption
exhibits.section: A receipt with no name on it
exhibits.action: Keep Private issuance selected; issue a token, redeem it at the origin, and compare the issuer and origin ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: The client verifies a P-384 DLEQ proof, finalizes a type-0x0001 token, the origin checks its authenticator and fresh nonce, and the collusion check reports no computable equality match for a properly blinded request.
exhibits.limits: All roles and the issuer secret run in one local browser session; no HTTP transport, attester, rate limiting, global key-consistency protocol, batched issuance or production service is implemented.

exhibits.title: Remove blinding and link issuance to redemption
exhibits.action: Choose BROKEN: remove blinding, issue the token, redeem it, then try to link the ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: Sets the blinding scalar to one; the issuer-observed raw input point equals the point derived from the redeemed token, and the UI draws one computed link and an alarm verdict.
exhibits.limits: An intentional local broken mode demonstrating direct point equality; it does not model probabilistic tracking, network metadata or a deployed Privacy Pass service.

exhibits.title: Link otherwise valid tokens by per-client issuer keys
exhibits.action: Choose BROKEN: per-client published key, select a roster size of two, three or four clients, issue and redeem their tokens, then link ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: Each client verifies a valid DLEQ proof under its own published key and redeems; the UI counts distinct key-ID buckets and draws one link per client partition.
exhibits.limits: A fixed local roster of two to four synthetic clients; valid per-client proofs alone do not establish that all clients saw the same globally published key.

exhibits.title: Reject an issuer response under an unpublished key
exhibits.action: Choose BROKEN: unpublished issuer key and click Issue token.
exhibits.outcome: A careful client verifies the DLEQ proof against the trusted published key and aborts before finalization; the page separately shows that a careless client's token would be refused by the origin configured with that trusted key.
exhibits.limits: The rogue issuer and careless client are intentionally local counterfactuals; this demonstrates checking the already trusted key, not global key-distribution or key-consistency infrastructure.

exhibits.title: Beam-splitter source model
exhibits.section: A beam-splitter QRNG — unpredictable by physics, imperfect by engineering
exhibits.action: Set detector mismatch and persistence, emit another stream, or stick detector B.
exhibits.outcome: Raw click bits and measured detector balance change; downstream entropy, extractor, and health panels update.
exhibits.limits: Photons are simulated using browser cryptographic randomness; this is not a connected physical QRNG or a source validation.

exhibits.title: Shannon versus min-entropy
exhibits.section: Shannon says “99.7% random.” Min-entropy says otherwise.
exhibits.action: Change source mismatch or persistence and inspect the live chart and attacker-work display.
exhibits.outcome: Measured Shannon and bias-based min-entropy diverge; a configured-model most-likely-path bound supplies the correlated block accounting.
exhibits.limits: Per-bit bias formulas assume independent bits; the correlated attacker-work figure depends on this synthetic source model, not an assessed hardware source.

exhibits.title: Von Neumann debiasing
exhibits.section: Von Neumann debiasing: perfect balance, brutal cost, wrong assumption
exhibits.action: Step bit pairs, run the rest, then make the source 80% streaky.
exhibits.outcome: See 01/10 kept, equal pairs discarded, throughput and output balance; a first-order predictor may expose dependence after debiasing.
exhibits.limits: Real pair processing on a simulated bitstream; first-order predictor is a diagnostic, not proof of unpredictability.

exhibits.title: Seeded Toeplitz extraction
exhibits.section: Toeplitz extraction — trading quantity for uniformity, with a receipt
exhibits.action: Set output length, draw a fresh seed, and extract; try exceeding the model min-entropy budget.
exhibits.outcome: A real GF(2) Toeplitz matrix-vector product displays output, seed/matrix, first-row parity, and Leftover Hash Lemma distance bound; a latched health alarm blocks extraction.
exhibits.limits: Input is simulated and k comes from its configured model; Toeplitz is not listed as a vetted SP 800-90B conditioning component; the displayed policy thresholds are teaching choices.

exhibits.title: Continuous RCT/APT monitor
exhibits.section: SP 800-90B health tests — because a dead source outputs a beautiful constant
exhibits.action: Stick and repair the detector, then explicitly recommission after an alarm.
exhibits.outcome: Continuous Repetition Count and Adaptive Proportion monitors show cutoffs, failures, and a latched boundary that blocks extractor input.
exhibits.limits: Health tests act on synthetic emissions and are tripwires for specified failures, not entropy estimators or source certification.

exhibits.title: Health-test threshold workshop
exhibits.section: The source has failed. Will your monitor notice?
exhibits.action: Choose failure mode and RCT/APT cutoffs or window, then test the setting.
